title: Two Sum Problem
prompt: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to target. You may assume that each input has exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice. Return the indices in any order.
hints: A brute-force check of all pairs takes O(N^2) time.
Can you store numbers seen so far in a hash map to look up (target - num) in O(1) time?

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
prompt: You are given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a given stock on the ith day. You want to maximize your profit by choosing a single day to buy one stock and choosing a different day in the future to sell that stock. Return the maximum profit you can achieve from this transaction. If you cannot achieve any profit, return 0.

examples.output: 5 (Buy day 2 at 1, sell day 5 at 6)

hints: Keep track of the minimum price observed so far as you iterate through the list.
At each step, calculate potential profit = current_price - min_price and update max_profit.

title: Contains Duplicate
prompt: Given an integer array nums, return true if any value appears at least twice in the array, and return false if every element is distinct.

examples.output: true
false

hints: A set or hash set allows O(1) average lookup and insertion.
Check if the element is already in the set; if yes, return true.

title: Longest Subarray with Sum K
prompt: Given an array of integers arr and an integer K, find the length of the longest sub-array having sum equal to K. The array can contain both positive and negative integers.

examples.output: 4 (Subarray [5, 2, 7, 1])

hints: Think about prefix sums. If prefix_sum[j] - prefix_sum[i] = K, then subarray between i+1 and j sums to K.
Use a hash map to record the first occurrence of each prefix sum.

title: Maximum Subarray (Kadane's Algorithm)
prompt: Given an integer array nums, find the subarray with the largest sum, and return its sum. A subarray is a contiguous non-empty sequence of elements within an array.
hints: At each index, decide whether to add current element to existing running sum or start fresh from current element.
current_sum = max(num, current_sum + num).

title: Product of Array Except Self
prompt: Given an integer array nums, return an array answer such that answer[i] is equal to the product of all the elements of nums except nums[i]. The algorithm must run in O(n) time and without using the division operation.
hints: Can you compute the product of all elements to the left of i, and product of all elements to the right of i?
Store prefix products in the result array, then traverse backwards maintaining suffix product.

title: Trapping Rain Water
prompt: Given n non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining.
hints: Water trapped at index i depends on min(max_left, max_right) - height[i].
You can solve this with precomputed left/right arrays or two pointers moving from outside inward.

title: First Missing Positive
prompt: Given an unsorted integer array nums, return the smallest positive integer that is not present in nums. You must implement an algorithm that runs in O(n) time and uses O(1) auxiliary space.
hints: The answer must lie between 1 and n + 1.
Can you place each number x in its correct index (x - 1) by swapping in-place?

title: Sliding Window Maximum
prompt: You are given an array of integers nums, and there is a sliding window of size k which is moving from the very left of the array to the very right. You can only see the k numbers in the window. Each time the sliding window moves right by one position, return the max sliding window.
hints: A monotonic decreasing deque can maintain indices of elements in the current window.
Remove indices outside the window from the front, and remove smaller elements from the back.

title: Valid Anagram
prompt: Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s, and false otherwise. An Anagram is a word or phrase formed by rearranging the letters of a different word or phrase, typically using all the original letters exactly once.

examples.output: true
false

hints: If lengths differ, they cannot be anagrams.
Count character frequencies using an array of size 26 or a hash map.

title: Valid Palindrome
prompt: A phrase is a palindrome if, after converting all uppercase letters into lowercase letters and removing all non-alphanumeric characters, it reads the same forward and backward. Alphanumeric characters include letters and numbers. Given a string s, return true if it is a palindrome, or false otherwise.

examples.input: s = 'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama'
examples.output: true
false

hints: Use two pointers, left starting at 0 and right at len(s) - 1.
Skip non-alphanumeric characters and compare lowercase values.

title: Longest Common Prefix
prompt: Write a function to find the longest common prefix string amongst an array of strings. If there is no common prefix, return an empty string ''.

examples.output: 'fl'

hints: Sort the strings and compare only the first and last strings.
Alternatively, iterate character by character across all strings.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
prompt: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without duplicate characters.
hints: Use a sliding window with left and right pointers.
Keep a hash map of characters to their most recent indices to jump the left pointer.

title: Group Anagrams
prompt: Given an array of strings strs, group the anagrams together. You can return the answer in any order.

examples.output: [['bat'],['nat','tan'],['ate','eat','tea']]

hints: Anagrams have the exact same sorted character sequence.
Use the sorted string or a character count tuple as a hash map key.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
prompt: Given a string s, return the longest palindromic substring in s.

examples.output: 'bab' (or 'aba')
'bb'

hints: Every palindrome has a center. There are 2n - 1 centers (odd and even length).
Expand outward from each center as long as characters match.

title: Minimum Window Substring
prompt: Given two strings s and t of lengths m and n respectively, return the minimum window substring of s such that every character in t (including duplicates) is included in the window. If there is no such substring, return the empty string ''.

examples.output: 'BANC'

hints: Use a sliding window with character frequency maps.
Expand the right pointer until all characters in t are satisfied, then shrink from the left to minimize.

title: Wildcard Matching
prompt: Given an input string (s) and a pattern (p), implement wildcard pattern matching with support for '?' and '*' where '?' matches any single character and '*' matches any sequence of characters (including the empty sequence).

examples.output: false
true
false

hints: Use 2D dynamic programming dp[i][j] representing if s[0..i] matches p[0..j].

title: Regular Expression Matching
prompt: Given an input string s and a pattern p, implement regular expression matching with support for '.' and '*' where '.' matches any single character and '*' matches zero or more of the preceding element.

examples.output: true
true

hints: Notice that '*' modifies the preceding character, never stands alone.
Use top-down memoization or bottom-up DP checking zero occurrences or one/more occurrences.

title: Binary Search
prompt: Given an array of integers nums which is sorted in ascending order, and an integer target, write a function to search target in nums. If target exists, then return its index. Otherwise, return -1. You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime complexity.
hints: Maintain low and high pointers. Compute mid = low + (high - low) // 2.
Narrow the search half based on comparing nums[mid] with target.

title: Merge Sorted Array
prompt: You are given two integer arrays nums1 and nums2, sorted in non-decreasing order, and two integers m and n, representing the number of elements in nums1 and nums2 respectively. Merge nums1 and nums2 into a single array sorted in non-decreasing order inside nums1 in-place.
hints: Fill nums1 from the back to avoid overwriting elements.
Use three pointers: p1 = m - 1, p2 = n - 1, and p = m + n - 1.

title: First Bad Version
prompt: Suppose you have n versions [1, 2, ..., n] and you want to find out the first bad one, which causes all the following ones to be bad. You are given an API bool isBadVersion(version) which returns whether version is bad. Implement a function to find the first bad version with minimum API calls.
hints: This is a classic binary search problem over monotonic boolean values: [F, F, F, T, T].
When isBadVersion(mid) is true, the first bad version is at mid or to the left.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
prompt: There is an integer array nums sorted in ascending order with distinct values. Prior to being passed to your function, nums is possibly rotated at an unknown pivot index. Given nums and an integer target, return the index of target if it is in nums, or -1 if it is not in nums in O(log n) time.
hints: In any rotated sorted array, at least one half (left or right of mid) is always sorted.
Determine which half is cleanly sorted, then check if target falls within that sorted half.

title: Find Peak Element
prompt: A peak element is an element that is strictly greater than its neighbors. Given a 0-indexed integer array nums, find a peak element, and return its index. If the array contains multiple peaks, return the index to any of the peaks in O(log n) time.
hints: If nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1], there must be a peak to the right.
If nums[mid] > nums[mid + 1], a peak exists at mid or to the left.

title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
prompt: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the kth largest element in the array. Note that it is the kth largest element in sorted order, not the kth distinct element. Can you solve it in O(n) average time?
hints: A min-heap of size k yields O(n log k) time.
QuickSelect algorithm with random pivoting yields O(n) average time.

title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
prompt: Given two sorted arrays nums1 and nums2 of size m and n respectively, return the median of the two sorted arrays. The overall run time complexity should be O(log (m+n)).
hints: Partition both arrays such that left halves contain (m + n + 1) // 2 elements.
Binary search on the smaller array for the partition cut position.

title: Merge k Sorted Lists
prompt: You are given an array of k linked-lists lists, each linked-list is sorted in ascending order. Merge all the linked-lists into one sorted linked-list and return it.
hints: Use a min-heap to store the head of each of the k lists.
Alternatively, use divide and conquer: pair up lists and merge each pair in O(N log k).

title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
prompt: Given an integer array nums, return an integer array counts where counts[i] is the number of smaller elements to the right of nums[i].
hints: Think about modified merge sort. During merging, when an element from right half is placed before left, it counts smaller elements.
Alternatively, use a Binary Indexed Tree (Fenwick Tree) or Segment Tree.

title: Explain the Four Pillars of OOP
prompt: Explain the four core principles of Object-Oriented Programming (Encapsulation, Abstraction, Inheritance, and Polymorphism). Provide code examples demonstrating each concept and discuss their practical advantages in software maintainability.

examples.output: Clear definition and real-world example (e.g. Vehicle hierarchy, BankAccount encapsulation)

hints: Encapsulation binds data and methods together and restricts direct access (private variables, getters/setters).
Abstraction hides implementation details (interfaces, abstract classes).
Inheritance promotes code reuse, and Polymorphism enables multiple forms (compile-time vs runtime).

title: Method Overloading vs Method Overriding
prompt: Explain the difference between method overloading and method overriding in object-oriented languages like Java, C++, or Python. Discuss compile-time vs runtime binding, rules regarding parameter lists and return types, and static methods.

examples.input: Overloading: add(int, int) vs add(int, int, int)
examples.output: Compile-time polymorphism
Run-time polymorphism via vtable

hints: Overloading happens within the same class with same name but different signatures.
Overriding occurs in derived classes with identical method signature.

title: Abstract Class vs Interface
prompt: Compare an Abstract Class and an Interface. When should you choose one over the other? Discuss default methods, multiple inheritance, state storage, and access modifiers across languages.

examples.output: Abstract class for common state/identity; interface for capabilities/contracts

hints: A class can implement multiple interfaces, but typically only inherit from one abstract class.
Abstract classes can have instance variables and constructors; interfaces define contracts.

title: Design a Singleton Pattern (Thread-Safe)
prompt: Explain the Singleton design pattern and provide a thread-safe implementation. Discuss lazy vs eager initialization, double-checked locking, potential memory model pitfalls, and why enums or static inner classes are preferred in modern development.

examples.output: Instance created exactly once even across concurrent threads

hints: Make constructor private to prevent instantiation.
In double-checked locking, ensure the instance variable is declared volatile to avoid instruction reordering.

title: Explain SOLID Design Principles with Examples
prompt: Detail the 5 SOLID principles of object-oriented design: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, and Dependency Inversion. For each, give an example of violation and how to refactor it cleanly.

examples.input: OrderService doing billing, email, and DB writes
examples.output: Violates SRP -> separate into OrderRepository, EmailNotifier, InvoiceGenerator

hints: SRP: A class should have only one reason to change.
OCP: Open for extension, closed for modification.
LSP: Subtypes must be substitutable for base types without breaking correctness.

title: Factory Method vs Abstract Factory Pattern
prompt: Compare the Factory Method pattern and the Abstract Factory pattern. Write an implementation scenario (such as a cross-platform UI toolkit with Windows/Mac Buttons and Checkboxes) showing when Abstract Factory is required.

examples.output: GUIFactory -> WinFactory, MacFactory producing WinButton, MacButton

hints: Factory Method uses inheritance and relies on derived classes to decide which class to instantiate.
Abstract Factory uses composition to produce families of related or dependent objects.

title: Design an Object-Oriented Parking Lot System
prompt: Design a Parking Lot system using object-oriented principles. The parking lot has multiple floors, different parking spot sizes (Motorcycle, Compact, Large), hourly fee calculation, ticket generation on entry, and payment processing on exit. Write class definitions with key methods.

examples.output: Class hierarchy: ParkingLot, Floor, Spot, Vehicle, Ticket, PaymentStrategy

hints: Model relationships: ParkingLot has-a List<Floor>; Floor has-a List<ParkingSpot>.
Vehicle hierarchy (Car, Bike, Truck) interacts with Spot assignment via polymorphism.

title: Design a Rate Limiter with OOP Principles
prompt: Design an in-memory Rate Limiter class using object-oriented design and design patterns. Support multiple rate limiting algorithms (Token Bucket, Sliding Window Log, Leaky Bucket) using Strategy pattern. Include client identification and thread safety.

examples.output: true if under limit, false if threshold exceeded

hints: Use the Strategy pattern to encapsulate different rate-limiting algorithms behind a common RateLimiterStrategy interface.
Ensure thread safety with lock-free atomics or ConcurrentHashMap.

title: Virtual Functions and Virtual Method Table (VTABLE)
prompt: Explain how runtime polymorphism and virtual functions are implemented under the hood in C++ or JVM languages. Detail the structure and mechanics of the VTABLE, the virtual table pointer (vptr), memory overhead, and what happens during a virtual method call.

examples.output: Dereferences vptr -> looks up speak() offset in Derived's vtable -> jumps to function pointer

hints: Each class with virtual functions has exactly one static vtable table containing function pointers.
Each instance carries a hidden vptr pointing to its class vtable.

title: Explain ACID Properties in DBMS
prompt: Explain ACID properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) in database transactions. Describe how each property prevents database anomalies and how DBMS mechanisms like Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) and locking achieve them.

examples.input: Bank transfer: deduct $100 from A, add $100 to B
examples.output: Either both happen or neither (Atomicity)

hints: Atomicity: All-or-nothing execution, maintained by undo logs.
Isolation: Concurrent transactions do not interfere; maintained by locks or MVCC.

title: Primary Key vs Unique Key vs Foreign Key
prompt: Differentiate between Primary Key, Unique Key, and Foreign Key constraints. Discuss nullability, indexing behavior, cascading updates/deletes, and referential integrity with SQL schema examples.

examples.input: Student(id PK, email UNIQUE, dept_id FK)
examples.output: Enforces entity integrity and referential integrity

hints: Primary key cannot be null and typically creates a clustered index.
Unique key allows one null (in most SQL engines) and creates non-clustered index.

title: Types of SQL Joins (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL, CROSS)
prompt: Explain and illustrate the differences between INNER JOIN, LEFT OUTER JOIN, RIGHT OUTER JOIN, FULL OUTER JOIN, and CROSS JOIN. Write SQL queries demonstrating each with sample output tables.

examples.input: Employees left join Departments on dept_id
examples.output: All employees included, even those without department (NULL)

hints: INNER JOIN returns only matching rows from both tables.
CROSS JOIN produces Cartesian product (m * n rows).

title: Database Normalization (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF)
prompt: Explain database normalization and each normal form from 1NF to BCNF. Provide an unnormalized relation with functional dependencies and show step-by-step decomposition into 3NF/BCNF while preserving dependencies.

examples.output: Decompose into Student, Course, StudentCourse to eliminate update/delete anomalies

hints: 1NF: Atomic values, no repeating groups.
2NF: In 1NF and no partial dependencies on composite primary key.
3NF: In 2NF and no transitive dependencies.

title: Clustered vs Non-Clustered Indexes and B+ Trees
prompt: Explain the architecture of Clustered vs Non-Clustered Indexes. Why do relational databases use B+ Trees instead of Binary Search Trees or Hash Tables for indexing? Discuss leaf node chaining and range queries.

examples.input: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE date BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-01-31'
examples.output: B+ Tree leaf linked-list traverses contiguous disk blocks in O(log N + K)

hints: Clustered index determines the physical order of data on disk (only 1 per table).
B+ tree stores all records in leaves with high fan-out, minimizing disk I/O seeks.

title: Transaction Isolation Levels and Read Phenomena
prompt: Detail the 4 ANSI SQL Transaction Isolation Levels (Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable). Explain the anomalies each level prevents: Dirty Read, Non-Repeatable Read, and Phantom Read.

examples.output: Transaction A reads uncommitted data written by Transaction B which later rolls back

hints: Read Committed avoids Dirty Reads using short-term read locks or snapshot views.
Repeatable Read prevents Non-Repeatable reads; Serializable prevents Phantom reads via range locks.

title: Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC)
prompt: How does Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) work in modern engines like PostgreSQL and MySQL InnoDB? Explain how readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers, tuple visibility checks using transaction IDs, and vacuum/purge processes.

examples.input: Concurrent long-running SELECT and high-frequency UPDATE
examples.output: SELECT sees snapshot from its start timestamp without taking exclusive locks

hints: Each row has hidden metadata columns like xmin/xmax or trx_id and roll_ptr.
Old versions are kept in undo logs or table pages until no active transaction needs them.

title: Two-Phase Locking (2PL) and Deadlock Detection
prompt: Explain the Strict Two-Phase Locking (Strict 2PL) protocol. Contrast the growing phase and shrinking phase. How does the DBMS detect deadlocks using Wait-For Graphs, and how does it resolve them using victim selection?

examples.input: T1 holds Lock A, needs Lock B; T2 holds Lock B, needs Lock A
examples.output: Wait-for graph cycle detected -> abort T1 or T2 with deadlock exception

hints: Growing phase: locks acquired, no locks released. Shrinking phase: locks released, none acquired.
Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until commit/abort to ensure recoverability.

title: Sharding vs Partitioning and Distributed Transactions
prompt: Contrast horizontal partitioning within a single database and horizontal sharding across distributed nodes. Explain the challenges of distributed transactions across shards and how the Two-Phase Commit (2PC) protocol guarantees atomicity.

examples.input: User data partitioned by hash(user_id) across 16 shards
examples.output: 2PC Coordinator coordinates Prepare and Commit phases with all participant shards

hints: Partitioning is managed locally by one engine; sharding distributes data across independent servers.
2PC has Prepare and Commit phases, but can block if coordinator crashes.

title: Process vs Thread
prompt: What is the difference between a process and a thread? Discuss memory address space, context switching overhead, communication mechanisms (IPC vs shared memory), and process control block (PCB) vs thread control block (TCB).

examples.input: Browser tabs vs background download thread
examples.output: Tabs run in isolated processes for fault-tolerance; threads share heap within a process

hints: Processes have independent memory address spaces; threads within the same process share heap, data, and code segments.
Thread context switch is faster because MMU virtual memory mappings do not need to be flushed.

title: CPU Scheduling Algorithms (FCFS, SJF, Round Robin)
prompt: Compare CPU scheduling algorithms: First-Come First-Served (FCFS), Shortest Job First (SJF), Priority Scheduling, and Round Robin (RR). Calculate average turnaround time and waiting time for a set of given burst times, and discuss convoy effect.

examples.input: Processes P1(burst=24), P2(burst=3), P3(burst=3) in FCFS vs RR(quantum=4)
examples.output: Round Robin prevents process starvation and minimizes response time

hints: SJF is optimal for minimizing average waiting time but requires future knowledge.
Round Robin is preemptive and fair for time-sharing systems.

title: What is a System Call and Context Switch?
prompt: Explain what a system call is and how user mode transitions to kernel mode. Detail the step-by-step sequence of hardware interrupts, saving CPU registers, trap handling, and context switching.

examples.input: read() or fork() executed in user code
examples.output: Triggers software interrupt (trap) -> CPU switches to ring 0 -> executes kernel dispatch table

hints: Dual-mode operation (User mode Ring 3 vs Kernel mode Ring 0) protects hardware.
System call triggers a trap instruction that switches privileges and executes the kernel handler.

title: Deadlock: Necessary Conditions and Banker's Algorithm
prompt: Explain Coffman's four necessary conditions for deadlock (Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait). Explain how Banker's algorithm detects a safe state and avoids deadlocks with allocation and need matrices.

examples.input: Total resources=[10,5,7], Current allocations and Max claims
examples.output: Determine safe sequence: <P1, P3, P0, P2, P4>

hints: Deadlock can only occur if ALL four Coffman conditions hold simultaneously.
Breaking any single condition (e.g. total ordering on resource acquisition) prevents deadlock.

title: Virtual Memory, Paging, and Page Faults
prompt: Explain the concept of Virtual Memory and Paging. Describe the address translation mechanism from Virtual Address to Physical Address using Page Tables, Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB), and what occurs step-by-step during a Page Fault.

examples.output: TLB lookup -> Page Table lookup -> Frame Number (f) -> Physical Address = [f | d]

hints: TLB acts as a high-speed hardware cache for page table lookups.
On page fault (valid bit = 0), OS trap halts process, reads page from swap disk, updates frame table, and restarts instruction.

title: Page Replacement Algorithms (FIFO, LRU, Optimal)
prompt: Compare Page Replacement algorithms: FIFO, Least Recently Used (LRU), and Belady's Optimal algorithm. Explain Belady's Anomaly where increasing the number of frames increases page faults in FIFO.

examples.output: FIFO page faults increase from 9 to 10 (Belady's Anomaly)

hints: LRU does not suffer from Belady's Anomaly because it is a stack algorithm.
LRU in practice is approximated using Clock algorithm (second-chance algorithm) with reference bits.

title: Inter-Process Communication (Pipes, Sockets, Shared Memory)
prompt: Contrast different Inter-Process Communication (IPC) mechanisms: Anonymous Pipes, Named Pipes (FIFOs), Message Queues, Shared Memory, and Sockets. Compare performance, synchronization requirements, and boundaries across machines.

examples.output: Shared Memory is fastest (zero copy) but requires explicit semaphores/mutexes for synchronization

hints: Shared memory avoids kernel buffer copying, making it the fastest IPC mechanism.
Sockets work across network boundaries between distinct physical hosts.

title: Semaphores vs Mutexes vs Spinlocks
prompt: Differentiate between Mutex, Counting Semaphore, and Spinlock. Explain Priority Inversion and how Priority Inheritance Protocol resolves it in real-time operating systems.

examples.input: Low priority task holds mutex, High priority task waits, Medium priority task preempts Low
examples.output: Priority Inversion: Medium delays High -> solved by elevating Low's priority to High

hints: Mutex is ownership-based locking (only the locker can unlock). Semaphore is a signaling mechanism.
Spinlocks busy-wait in a loop; useful only for very short waits on multi-core CPUs without thread suspension.

title: Linux CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler) and cgroups
prompt: Explain the architecture of Linux Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS). How does it use virtual runtime (vruntime) and red-black trees to balance CPU allocation? Discuss how Linux cgroups and namespaces form the foundation of containerization (Docker).

examples.output: CFS always picks the leftmost node in the red-black tree (lowest vruntime)

hints: CFS tracks vruntime: CPU time scaled by nice level weight.
cgroups control resource limits (CPU, memory, I/O) while namespaces provide isolation (pid, net, mount).

title: OSI 7-Layer Model vs TCP/IP Model
prompt: Compare the OSI 7-layer model and the TCP/IP model. Detail the functions and standard protocols operating at each layer (Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application).

examples.output: HTTP (Application) -> TCP (Transport) -> IP (Network) -> 802.11 Frame (Data Link) -> Radio Signal (Physical)

hints: TCP/IP merges Application, Presentation, and Session into Application layer.
Network layer handles routing (IP, ICMP); Transport layer handles end-to-end delivery (TCP, UDP).

title: TCP vs UDP
prompt: Explain the fundamental differences between TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and UDP (User Datagram Protocol). Discuss connection orientation, reliability, ordering, flow/congestion control, header size, and ideal use cases for each.

examples.input: Web page loading vs live multiplayer gaming stream
examples.output: Web uses TCP (requires no packet loss); gaming uses UDP (low latency, packet loss acceptable)

hints: TCP provides reliable, ordered byte-stream delivery via ACKs and retransmissions.
UDP is connectionless and lightweight (8-byte header vs 20-60 byte TCP header).

title: What Happens When You Type a URL in Browser?
prompt: Explain in detail every step that occurs when you type 'https://www.google.com' in a browser and press Enter. Cover DNS resolution, TCP 3-way handshake, TLS handshake, HTTP GET request, server response, and browser rendering pipeline.

examples.output: Browser cache -> OS DNS cache -> Recursive Resolver -> TCP SYN/ACK -> TLS 1.3 Key Exchange -> HTTP/2 Request -> DOM tree

hints: DNS check follows: browser cache -> OS hosts/cache -> router -> ISP recursive resolver -> root -> TLD -> authoritative.
TLS negotiation agrees on cipher suite and establishes symmetric session keys.

title: TCP 3-Way Handshake and 4-Way Teardown
prompt: Explain the TCP 3-way connection establishment (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) and 4-way termination (FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK). Explain sequence and acknowledgment numbering and why the TIME_WAIT state is necessary.

examples.output: Client sends SYN(seq=x) -> Server replies SYN(seq=y)+ACK(x+1) -> Client sends ACK(y+1)

hints: Initial sequence numbers are randomized to prevent spoofing and old duplicate packet confusion.
TIME_WAIT (usually 2*MSL) ensures the final ACK reaches server and old duplicate segments die out in network.

title: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3
prompt: Compare HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 (QUIC). Discuss Head-of-Line (HoL) blocking at application vs transport layers, binary framing, multiplexing over single TCP connection, server push, and UDP-based QUIC connection migration.

examples.output: HTTP/1.1 needs multiple TCP sockets; HTTP/2 multiplexes streams on 1 TCP; HTTP/3 eliminates TCP HoL blocking with QUIC

hints: HTTP/1.1 suffered from application-level HoL blocking.
HTTP/2 multiplexes over single TCP, but a dropped TCP packet stalls all streams. HTTP/3 solves this over UDP.

title: TCP Congestion Control (Slow Start, Congestion Avoidance)
prompt: Explain how TCP controls network congestion. Detail Slow Start, Congestion Avoidance, Fast Retransmit, and Fast Recovery phases. Explain the roles of Congestion Window (cwnd), Advertised Window (rwnd), and ssthresh.

examples.input: Packet loss detected via 3 duplicate ACKs
examples.output: Fast Retransmit sends missing packet immediately; ssthresh = cwnd / 2; cwnd = ssthresh + 3 (Fast Recovery)

hints: Slow start exponentially increases cwnd every RTT until ssthresh is reached.
After ssthresh, congestion avoidance linearly increases cwnd (+1 MSS per RTT).

title: How DNS Resolution Works (Recursive vs Iterative)
prompt: Explain the architecture of the Domain Name System (DNS). Compare recursive and iterative queries. Detail the roles of Root Name Servers, TLD Name Servers, and Authoritative Name Servers, plus DNS record types (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT).

examples.output: Root gives .com TLD -> TLD gives example.com auth server -> Auth server returns IP

hints: Recursive query: client asks resolver to do all lookup work and return final answer.
Iterative query: server returns best referral pointer to next name server.

title: TLS 1.3 Handshake and Symmetric/Asymmetric Encryption
prompt: Explain the cryptographic handshake of TLS 1.3. How does it achieve 1-RTT (and 0-RTT resumption) compared to TLS 1.2's 2-RTT? Detail Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral key exchange, digital certificates, and Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS).

examples.output: ServerHello returns server key_share -> both compute shared secret -> encrypted traffic begins in 1-RTT

hints: Asymmetric cryptography (RSA/ECC) verifies server identity; symmetric cryptography (AES-GCM/ChaCha20) encrypts data.
PFS ensures compromise of long-term server private key cannot decrypt past recorded sessions.

title: NAT (Network Address Translation) and BGP Routing
prompt: Explain Network Address Translation (NAT) and Port Address Translation (PAT/NAPT). Discuss private IP ranges (RFC 1918) and how NAT enables IPv4 survival. At the Internet scale, explain how BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) routes traffic between Autonomous Systems (AS).

examples.output: Router rewrites source to Public IP:60001 and maps response back via NAT state table

hints: PAT maps many internal private IPs to a single public IP by altering source port numbers.
BGP is a path-vector protocol exchanging AS-PATH attributes between Autonomous Systems.

title: Tell Me About Yourself and Your Engineering Journey
prompt: Craft a structured 2-minute elevator pitch answering 'Tell me about yourself'. Frame your response using the Past-Present-Future formula: your background/education, current projects and technical passions, and why you are excited for this specific role.

examples.output: Past (Computer Science foundations) -> Present (Full-stack web apps, algorithms, OJT project) -> Future (Contributing to scalable products here)

hints: Keep it under 2 minutes. Do not recite your resume line by line.
Focus on tangible technical achievements, curiosity, and alignment with the company mission.

title: What Are Your Greatest Strengths and Weaknesses?
prompt: How do you answer 'What are your strengths and weaknesses?' without sounding clichéd? Provide an authentic technical strength with evidence, and a genuine area of improvement along with proactive steps you are currently taking to overcome it.

examples.output: Real weakness: Hesitant to delegate or getting stuck perfecting code -> Action: Implementing time-boxing and early PR reviews

hints: Avoid fake weaknesses like 'I work too hard' or 'I am too much of a perfectionist'.
Pair your weakness with active remediation steps and measurable progress.

title: Why Do You Want to Work at Our Company?
prompt: Explain how you research and structure an answer to 'Why this company?'. Connect company engineering blogs, open source contributions, product architecture, and company culture to your personal career aspirations.

examples.output: Specific mention of company's technical challenge (e.g. low-latency order matching or open-source libraries) and cultural fit

hints: Show you did your homework: cite specific engineering initiatives or products.
Explain what you bring to the table, not just what the company gives you.

title: Tell Me About a Time You Faced a Technical Conflict (STAR Method)
prompt: Using the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result), describe a scenario where you had a strong technical disagreement with a teammate or mentor regarding an architecture or framework choice. How did you navigate the conversation to reach consensus?

examples.input: Disagreement on REST vs GraphQL for mobile client
examples.output: Conducted benchmark spike, compared payload sizes and bandwidth constraints, aligned on data-driven decision

hints: Situation (20%): Context and problem.
Task (10%): Your specific responsibility.
Action (50%): What you did, how you communicated, gathered data, and stayed objective.
Result (20%): Outcome, team morale, and key lesson learned.

title: Describe a Time You Failed or Made a Critical Mistake
prompt: Describe a project or technical failure you experienced. What went wrong, how did you take immediate ownership, what root-cause analysis did you conduct, and what preventive safeguards did you put in place to ensure it never happens again?

examples.input: Accidentally deployed buggy code or dropped a test database table
examples.output: Took ownership, communicated immediately, implemented automated rollback scripts and pre-commit checks

hints: Senior engineers value extreme ownership and blameless post-mortem learning.
Focus heavily on the resolution, emotional resilience, and system safeguards added.

title: How Do You Handle Tight Deadlines and Shifting Priorities?
prompt: How do you manage your time and prioritize tasks when faced with tight deadlines, unexpected blockers, or shifting product requirements? Detail your approach to scope reduction, communicating with stakeholders, and avoiding burnout.

examples.input: 2 days before submission, major feature requirement changed
examples.output: Prioritized MVP core path, deferred non-essential UI animations, communicated transparent trade-offs

hints: Demonstrate prioritization frameworks (e.g. Eisenhower matrix, MoSCoW).
Emphasize proactive communication with leads before deadlines are missed.

title: Where Do You See Yourself in 5 Years as an Engineer?
prompt: Answer 'Where do you see yourself in 5 years?'. Balance technical depth (mastering systems, architecture, distributed computing) with leadership and mentorship, illustrating how you plan to grow in impact and responsibility.

examples.output: From proficient junior engineer delivering independent modules -> to senior engineer designing robust architectures and mentoring juniors

hints: Demonstrate commitment to continuous learning and technical mastery.
Express a desire to take on greater architectural responsibility and mentor junior team members.

title: Tell Me About a Time You Had to Learn a Technology Very Quickly
prompt: Describe a scenario where you were assigned a task or project requiring a framework, language, or tool you had never used before. How did you structure your learning under pressure, build the solution, and deliver it successfully?

examples.input: Learning Bootstrap 5 or WebSocket protocol in 48 hours for hackathon
examples.output: Read official documentation, built minimal prototype proof-of-concept, integrated into team repository

hints: Highlight your self-learning methodology: official docs, building miniature test spikes, debugging systematically.
Show speed, curiosity, and high agency.

title: Do You Have Any Questions for Us? (Reverse Interviewing)
prompt: What questions should you ask the interviewer at the end of a software engineering interview? Provide 4 thoughtful, high-impact questions spanning engineering culture, deployment practices, mentoring, and technical vision.

examples.input: Interviewer asks: 'Do you have questions for me?'
examples.output: 1. What does a typical deployment day look like? 2. How are technical debt vs feature requests balanced? 3. What separates good engineers from great ones on this team?

hints: Never say 'No, you covered everything'.
Ask questions that reveal team culture, engineering velocity, and mentorship practices.
